about: Sourced life stories for the fourteen apostles. Written from Scripture and the reviewed dossiers Research/People/apostles-1.md and Research/People/apostles-2.md.

peter-mat-4-18.short: A fisherman from Bethsaida whom Jesus named Cephas, or Peter; named first in every list of the Twelve, he denied Jesus three times and spoke for the apostles.

paragraphs.text: Simon was the son of a man the KJV calls Jona or Jonas, and his brother was Andrew. John's Gospel says they came from Bethsaida, and Mark tells of "the house of Simon and Andrew" at Capernaum. Simon was married: Jesus healed "Simon's wife's mother" in that house, and Paul later writes of Cephas taking "a wife" with him on his travels. Scripture does not give her name.

John's Gospel tells how Andrew found his brother first and told him, "We have found the Messias". When Jesus saw Simon he said, "thou shalt be called Cephas". Matthew and Mark tell how Jesus later saw the two brothers casting a net into the sea of Galilee and called them to be "fishers of men", and they left their nets and followed him. Luke tells it with a great catch of fish, at which Simon fell at Jesus' knees and said, "Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord".

He is named first in every list of the Twelve. With James and John he was one of three whom Jesus took into Jairus's house, up a high mountain where he was transfigured, and with him in Gethsemane. Near Caesarea Philippi he said, "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God", and Jesus answered, "thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church". When Jesus then began to speak of his coming death, Peter rebuked him, and Jesus said, "Get thee behind me, Satan".

On the night of the arrest Jesus told him, "before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice". Peter cut off the right ear of the high priest's servant, Malchus. Then, in the high priest's house, he three times denied knowing Jesus, and when the cock crew he "went out, and wept bitterly". On the morning of the resurrection the angel at the tomb said, "tell his disciples and Peter", and Paul writes that the risen Christ "was seen of Cephas".

By the sea of Tiberias the risen Jesus asked him three times, "lovest thou me?", and each time told him to feed his lambs or his sheep. He also told Peter that when he was old, another would "carry thee whither thou wouldest not", and John adds that this signified "by what death he should glorify God". Scripture does not say where or how he died.

At Pentecost, "standing up with the eleven", he preached to the crowd in Jerusalem. Acts tells of him healing a lame man with John, answering the council, and going to the centurion Cornelius at Caesarea; Herod later put him in prison, and an angel led him out. Acts last names him at the council in Jerusalem, and Paul writes that at Antioch he "withstood him to the face". Two letters of the New Testament open with his name.

andrew-mat-4-18.short: Simon Peter's brother, a fisherman from Bethsaida, who followed Jesus from John the Baptist and brought his brother to him.

paragraphs.text: Andrew was a disciple of John the Baptist. When John looked at Jesus and said, "Behold the Lamb of God", Andrew and another disciple followed Jesus and stayed with him that day. Andrew then found his own brother Simon, told him, "We have found the Messias", and brought him to Jesus.

He and Simon came from Bethsaida and fished together on the sea of Galilee. Matthew and Mark tell how Jesus saw the two brothers casting a net and called them, and they left their nets and followed him. Mark tells of "the house of Simon and Andrew" at Capernaum, where Jesus healed Simon's wife's mother. Andrew is named in every list of the Twelve.

John's Gospel names him twice more. Before the feeding of the five thousand he said, "There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes". When some Greeks asked Philip to see Jesus, Philip told Andrew, and the two of them told Jesus. With Peter, James and John he asked Jesus privately, on the mount of Olives, when the temple's stones would be thrown down.
He was with the Eleven in the upper room in Jerusalem. Scripture says nothing more of him after that, and nothing of his death.

james-mat-4-21.short: Son of Zebedee, brother of John and a fisherman; one of three Jesus took aside, and the one apostle Scripture says was put to death.

paragraphs.text: James was a son of Zebedee. He and his brother John were in a ship with their father, mending their nets, when Jesus called them, and they left their father Zebedee "in the ship with the hired servants" and went after him. Luke says the two brothers were partners with Simon. Their mother is called "the mother of Zebedee's children"; she was among the women who watched the crucifixion from afar.

Jesus named James and John "Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder". With Peter, they were the three he took into Jairus's house, up a high mountain where he was transfigured, and with him in Gethsemane. When a Samaritan village would not receive Jesus, James and John asked whether they should command fire to come down from heaven, and Jesus turned and rebuked them.

In Matthew, their mother asked that her two sons might sit at Jesus' right hand and left in his kingdom; in Mark, the brothers ask it themselves. Jesus told them, "Ye shall indeed drink of the cup that I drink of".

After the resurrection "the sons of Zebedee" were by the sea of Tiberias when Jesus showed himself there, and James was with the Eleven in the upper room. Later "Herod the king" killed "James the brother of John with the sword". Of the Twelve he is the only one whose putting to death Scripture records. It does not say why Herod chose him, or where he was buried.

john-mat-4-21.short: A fisherman on the sea of Galilee, son of Zebedee and brother of James; with Peter and James, one of three Jesus took aside.

paragraphs.text: John and his brother James were in a ship with their father Zebedee, mending their nets, when Jesus called them; they left their father "in the ship with the hired servants" and went after him. Luke says the brothers were partners with Simon. Their mother asked Jesus that her two sons might sit at his right hand and left in his kingdom, and she was among the women who watched the crucifixion from afar.

Jesus named John and James "Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder". With Peter they were the three he took into Jairus's house, up a high mountain where he was transfigured, and with him in Gethsemane. John once told Jesus of a man casting out devils in his name, "and we forbad him", and Jesus answered, "Forbid him not". He and James asked whether to call down fire on a Samaritan village, and Jesus rebuked them.

Jesus sent Peter and John to prepare the passover. John's Gospel never uses his name. It speaks instead of an unnamed "disciple whom Jesus loved", who leaned on Jesus at the supper, stood by the cross and took Jesus' mother "unto his own home", and who "wrote these things". Scripture does not say whether that disciple was John.

After the resurrection he was with the Eleven in the upper room. He went up to the temple with Peter, where a lame man was healed, and the council marvelled at "the boldness of Peter and John", seeing that they were "unlearned and ignorant men". The apostles sent the two of them to Samaria, and on the way back they preached in many villages of the Samaritans.

A saying went round that the disciple whom Jesus loved would not die, but John's Gospel answers that Jesus had not said so. The writer of Revelation calls himself John and says he was in the isle of Patmos "for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ"; Scripture does not say whether he is the son of Zebedee. Scripture does not record John's death.

philip-mat-10-3.short: One of the Twelve, from Bethsaida; Jesus found him and called him, and Philip brought Nathanael to meet Jesus.

paragraphs.text: Philip was from Bethsaida, "the city of Andrew and Peter". John's Gospel tells that Jesus found him and said, "Follow me". Philip then found Nathanael and told him they had found the one of whom Moses and the prophets wrote; when Nathanael asked, "Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?", Philip answered, "Come and see".

Matthew, Mark and Luke name him only in their lists of the Twelve, where he is always fifth. In John's Gospel, before the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus asked Philip, "Whence shall we buy bread, that these may eat?", and Philip answered that two hundred pennyworth of bread would not be enough. When some Greeks came to him saying, "Sir, we would see Jesus", Philip told Andrew, and the two of them told Jesus.

When Jesus spoke of the Father, Philip asked, "Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us", and Jesus answered, "he that hath seen me hath seen the Father". Philip was with the Eleven in the upper room. Scripture gives him no family or trade, and says nothing of him after that.
Acts also tells of another Philip, one of seven men chosen in Jerusalem for "the daily ministration", whom it later calls "the evangelist". He is a different man from the apostle.

bartholomew-mat-10-3.short: One of the Twelve, known in Scripture only by his name in the lists of the apostles.

paragraphs.text: Bartholomew is named in every list of the Twelve: straight after Philip in Matthew, Mark and Luke, and after Thomas in Acts. Luke says Jesus chose the twelve from his disciples after a night of prayer and named them apostles. Scripture records no word or deed of Bartholomew by that name, and gives him no home, family or trade.
He was among the twelve whom Jesus sent out to preach and to heal, and he was with the Eleven in the upper room in Jerusalem. Scripture says nothing of him after that.
John's Gospel never uses the name Bartholomew, and the other Gospels never use the name Nathanael, the man Philip brought to Jesus. Scripture does not say whether the two are the same man.

thomas-mat-10-3.short: One of the Twelve, called Didymus, who would not believe the others' report of the risen Jesus until he saw Jesus himself eight days later.

paragraphs.text: Thomas is named in every list of the Twelve. John's Gospel three times adds that he was "called Didymus". Scripture gives him no home, family or trade.

When Jesus said they would go back into Judaea, to Lazarus who had died, Thomas said to the other disciples, "Let us also go, that we may die with him". Later, when Jesus spoke of going away to prepare a place, Thomas said, "Lord, we know not whither thou goest; and how can we know the way?", and Jesus answered, "I am the way, the truth, and the life".

Thomas was not with the others when the risen Jesus first came to them. He told them, "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails ... I will not believe". Eight days later Jesus came again and told Thomas to reach out his hand, and Thomas answered, "My Lord and my God". Jesus said, "blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed".
He was with Peter, Nathanael and others on the sea of Tiberias when the risen Jesus showed himself there, and he was with the Eleven in the upper room. Scripture says nothing of him after that.

matthew-mat-9-9.short: A tax collector whom Jesus called from his place at the receipt of custom; Mark and Luke call him Levi.

paragraphs.text: Matthew's Gospel tells that Jesus saw "a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom" and said, "Follow me", and he arose and followed him. Mark and Luke tell the same call of a publican they name Levi, and Mark calls him "Levi the son of Alphaeus". Luke adds that he "left all, rose up, and followed him".

Luke says Levi then made Jesus "a great feast in his own house", where many publicans and others sat at the table. When the Pharisees complained, Jesus answered, "I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance".

In Matthew's list of the Twelve he is "Matthew the publican"; Mark, Luke and Acts list him as Matthew, and none of the lists names a Levi. He was sent out with the Twelve and was with the Eleven in the upper room. Scripture records no words of his and says nothing of him after that.

james-mat-10-3.short: One of the Twelve, named in every list as James the son of Alphaeus; Scripture records nothing he said or did.

paragraphs.text: James the son of Alphaeus is named in all four lists of the Twelve, always ninth. He was among the twelve Jesus chose after a night of prayer and sent out to preach, and he was with the Eleven in the upper room.
Scripture tells very little about him. It gives him no home, trade or calling, records nothing he said or did, and says nothing of where he went or how he died.

Mark names a Mary as "the mother of James the less", and Paul writes of "James the Lord's brother", but Scripture never says that either of these is the son of Alphaeus. Mark also calls Levi the tax collector "the son of Alphaeus"; Scripture does not say whether this is the same Alphaeus.

judas-mat-10-3.short: Named Thaddaeus in the lists of Matthew and Mark; Luke and Acts have no Thaddaeus but list "Judas the brother of James"; Scripture says little more.

paragraphs.text: Matthew lists "Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus", and Mark lists "Thaddaeus". Luke and Acts have no Thaddaeus, but list "Judas the brother of James".

John's Gospel records one question from a disciple named "Judas ... not Iscariot": "how is it that thou wilt manifest thyself unto us, and not unto the world?" Jesus answered that if a man loves him he will keep his words, and that he and the Father will come to him. John does not say more of who this Judas was.

He was chosen with the Twelve and sent out with them, and he was with the Eleven in the upper room. Scripture says very little about him: no home, family or trade, and nothing after that. The letter of Jude is from "Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James"; Scripture does not say whether that Jude is this apostle.

simon-mat-10-4.short: One of the Twelve, called Simon the Canaanite by Matthew and Mark and Simon Zelotes by Luke and Acts; nothing he said or did is recorded.

paragraphs.text: Simon is named in every list of the Twelve. Matthew and Mark call him "Simon the Canaanite", Luke "Simon called Zelotes", and Acts "Simon Zelotes". Scripture does not explain either name.

He was chosen with the Twelve and sent out with them, and he was with the Eleven in the upper room. Scripture says very little about him: it records nothing he said or did, and gives no home, family, travels or death for him.
Luke's list names him beside Simon "whom he also named Peter", so he is a different man. Mark names a Simon among the brothers of Jesus; Scripture does not say whether that Simon is this one.

judas-mat-10-4.short: One of the Twelve, the son of Simon, who kept the disciples' money and betrayed Jesus to the chief priests for thirty pieces of silver.

paragraphs.text: Judas Iscariot was the son of Simon. He was chosen as one of the Twelve, and each Gospel list of the Twelve names him last, as the one who betrayed Jesus. John says he "was a thief, and had the bag", and carried what was put in it.

John's Gospel says Jesus knew "from the beginning" who would betray him, and that he said of the Twelve, "one of you is a devil", speaking of Judas. At Bethany, when Mary anointed Jesus' feet, Judas asked why the ointment was not sold for three hundred pence and given to the poor.

Judas went to the chief priests and asked, "What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you?", and they agreed on thirty pieces of silver. Luke and John say that Satan entered into him. At the supper Jesus said one of them would betray him and gave Judas the sop; Judas went out, "and it was night". In the garden he came with a crowd from the chief priests and kissed Jesus as the agreed sign.

Scripture tells of his death twice, in two different ways. Matthew says that when Judas saw Jesus condemned he "repented himself" and brought back the silver, saying, "I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood"; he cast it down in the temple, "and went and hanged himself", and the chief priests used the money to buy the potter's field. Acts, in Peter's words, says that he "purchased a field with the reward of iniquity; and falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst", and that the field was called Aceldama, "The field of blood". Mark, Luke's Gospel and John do not tell of his death.

Peter told the believers that the Scripture had to be fulfilled concerning Judas, for "he was numbered with us", and he quoted the Psalms: "his bishoprick let another take". Matthias was then chosen by lot to take his place.

matthias-act-1-23.short: The disciple chosen by lot to take the place of Judas Iscariot among the apostles; Scripture names him only on that day.

paragraphs.text: After Judas's death Peter said that one must be chosen from the men who had been with them "all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us", from the baptism of John until he was taken up, to be "a witness with us of his resurrection". Two were put forward: Joseph called Barsabas, surnamed Justus, and Matthias.

The believers prayed that the Lord would show which of the two he had chosen, and gave forth their lots, "and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles". Afterwards Acts speaks of "the twelve", but it never names Matthias again, and the Gospels never name him at all. Scripture records nothing he said or did, or where he went or how he died.

paul-act-7-58.short: Saul of Tarsus, a Pharisee who persecuted the church until the risen Jesus met him near Damascus; as Paul he carried the gospel to the Gentiles.

paragraphs.text: Saul was a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, and a Roman citizen by birth: "I was free born". He was of the tribe of Benjamin, "an Hebrew of the Hebrews", and a Pharisee, "the son of a Pharisee". He was brought up in Jerusalem "at the feet of Gamaliel". He worked with his own hands as a tentmaker, and his sister's son once warned him of a plot against his life.

He first appears at the stoning of Stephen, where the witnesses laid down their clothes "at a young man's feet, whose name was Saul", and he was "consenting unto his death". He then "made havock of the church", entering house after house and putting men and women in prison. He later wrote that he had persecuted the church of God.

On the road to Damascus a light from heaven shone round him, and a voice said, "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" When he asked who it was, the answer came, "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest". He was three days without sight, until Ananias came to him; then he was baptized. Acts tells this three times, once as the story of Acts and twice in Paul's own speeches, and the tellings differ in some details. In his letter to the Galatians Paul says God "called me by his grace", and that he went into Arabia.

Acts first calls him Paul at Paphos: "Saul, (who also is called Paul,)". With Barnabas, and later with Silas and Timothy, he went from city to city, preaching in the synagogues and turning to the Gentiles. He lists his own sufferings: "Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck". He also writes of "a thorn in the flesh" that the Lord did not take away, saying to him, "My grace is sufficient for thee".

In Jerusalem he was seized in the temple, and the chief captain of the band took him. He was held two years at Caesarea, appealed to Caesar, and was sent to Rome, coming through a shipwreck on the way. Acts ends with him in Rome for "two whole years in his own hired house", preaching "with all confidence, no man forbidding him".

In 2 Timothy he writes as a prisoner in Rome: "the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith". Scripture does not record his death. Many of the New Testament's letters, from Romans to Philemon, open with his name.
